newsitem.title: GERMANY: Weather brings concern as German harvest nears end.
newsitem.headline: Weather brings concern as German harvest nears end.

text.p: Germany's 1996 grain crop is on course for a high volume, but changeable weather is bringing concern over qualities and drying costs, farm sources said.
The rainy pattern has continued to disrupt harvest efforts and the next days should bring more showers and slightly colder temperatures, delaying completion into mid-September.
"Wheat volumes are high because of area expansions and recent rains have not really hurt the quality, but rye falling counts are worryingly low in some regions," one analyst said.
"This may bring a higher feed rye crop than anticipated."
Other analysts said feed rye might then replace other feedgrains and meals while bread rye could cost a premium.

The costs of drying grain mechanically at country merchants and co-ops would not necessarily drive new crop prices much higher, but one side-effect would be that farmers would need to part with their grain earlier and would store less.
"Once country merchants and co-ops have their hands on the grain, it does not make sense to transport it back to the farm," said a farm official in Germany's south.
Rye falling numbers, which measure milling qualities by falling times in seconds, have fallen in places below 100/120 as wet rye sprouted prematurely, disqualifying it for flour use.
Latest trade estimates put this year's grain crop at above 40 million tonnes, up from last year's 39.9 million. The farm ministry is due to issue preliminary results on Thursday.
Following is a region-by-region update --
WESTERN GERMANY
Wheat yields on the Rhine varied widely between six and nine tonnes/hectare. Wheat cutting was complete and 80 percent of rye had been brought in with satisfactory qualities.
The Bonn agricultural chamber said only late rye had low falling numbers. Malting barley yields and qualities were high.
Traders said low wheat hagberg numbers were noticeable in Rhineland-Palatinate, Hesse and Baden Wuerttemberg, and rye was also negatively affected.
Barley yields were down by around 14 percent.
Farmers in Westphalia said barley yields were high and wheat should also be good at 8.5-9.0 tonnes/ha. Rye yields also looked good at 8.0-8.5 tonnes but falling numbers were only 60-100.
SOUTHERN GERMANY
Wheat harvesting was mostly complete, with qualities and yields looking satisfactory, the Bavarian farm ministry said.
Traders put wheat at 12-14 percent protein and quoted wheat hagbergs in a wide 220-380 range. Early rye falling counts were 120-200 but later rye was between just 60 and 120.
"We advise farmers against speculative retention and hope they will market the wheat continously as other European countries seem to have some quality gaps," a spokesman said.
Protein content was generally high, which was good news for bread uses of wheat and rye but less so for malting barley, which must not be too high in protein.
NORTHERN GERMANY
Farmers in the north of Lower Saxony had almost completed harvests but grain in southern regions still needed to be cut.
A farm union source said the result should be "average", with wheat on light soils stressed by drought in the spring and barley yields down by 10-15 percent due to winter damage.
Some rye, which was stored wet, may show falling counts around 70, but generally results below 120 were "exceptional", the source said. There were also spikes at 250.
Some 70 to 80 percent of wheat had been brought in, with yields looking steady or slightly lower.
Harvesting in Schleswig-Holstein was in full swing, with some concern over low protein levels in wheat. But in rye there were surprisingly good qualities, good falling numbers and low ergot levels.
EASTERN GERMANY
The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern said winter barley yields were 4.55 tonnes per ha on average (6.78 in 1995) but differed widely after winter kill and drought.
Spring barley yields were high at 5.06 tonnes/ha on average (4.73).
Winter wheat samples pointed to possible yields of 6.21 tonnes/ha (6.82) and spring wheat samples at 5.05 (4.39).
Rye was seen at 4.97 tonnes/ha (5.42), with winter varieties highest, and oats at 4.57 tonnes/ha (4.83).
Rye falling numbers in this most northern states topped 180 but elsewhere in former East Germany farmers bemoaned levels below 100.
Wheat harvests in eastern Germany had only just begun and farmers were still cutting rye, triticale and spring barley.
